summary: Describes how to carry audio compressed with the BroadVoice narrowband and wideband speech codecs in RTP packets. The narrowband codec BV16 was chosen by CableLabs for PacketCable 1.5. It also covers use with MIME and SDP. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Voice is squeezed with a special coder to fit in small packets. This memo says how to put the squeezed voice in packets and how to describe it.

questions: how many bytes is a bv32 frame
how to describe bv16 in sdp
subtitle: How BroadVoice16 and BroadVoice32 speech frames ride inside RTP packets, with MIME and SDP details.

tldr.problem: The BroadVoice speech codecs needed a standard way to be carried in RTP packets and described in MIME and SDP.
tldr.mechanism: Each 5 ms frame is a fixed size (10 octets for BV16, 20 for BV32) sent with no extra payload header, with one or more consecutive whole frames per packet.
tldr.outcome: The RFC registers audio/BV16 and audio/BV32 and maps them to SDP. Frame counts are found by dividing the payload length by the frame size.

today: RFC 4298 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2005, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
RFC 4298 specifies how to send BroadVoice encoded speech or audio using the Real-time Transport Protocol (RFC 3550). A sender may put one or more codec frames in each packet depending on network conditions, bandwidth, delay needs and packet-loss tolerance.

BroadVoice is a speech codec family for VoIP, including Voice over Cable, Voice over DSL and IP phones. BV16 encodes 8 kHz narrowband speech at 16 kbit/s and BV32 encodes 16 kHz wideband speech at 32 kbit/s. Both use a 5 ms frame with no look ahead, so VoIP systems can have very low delay. BV16 was selected by CableLabs as a mandatory codec in PacketCable 1.5, while BV32 had not yet appeared in a public specification.
sections.plainLanguage: BroadVoice is a way to shrink a voice into small chunks, one every 5 thousandths of a second, so a phone call has very little lag.

sections.title: The RTP Payload
sections.content:
No payload header specific to this format is required: the RTP payload is simply one or more codec frames following the RTP header. The RTP timestamp MUST use units of 1/8000 of a second for BV16 and 1/16000 of a second for BV32, and it indicates the sampling instant of the oldest sample in the first frame.

With silence compression, the first packet after a silence period SHOULD have the RTP marker bit set to one. All other packets have it zero, and applications without silence suppression MUST set it to zero. The RTP payload type is outside the scope of the RFC; a profile may assign one, or a dynamic one is chosen.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet is an envelope holding a stack of voice slices. There is no extra label, just the slices.

sections.title: Frame Bit Layouts
sections.content:
A BV16 frame covers 40 samples at 8000 samples per second and is encoded as 80 bits, or 10 octets, octet-aligned with no padding. The bits are 14 for the Line Spectrum Pairs (7+7), 7 for pitch lag, 5 for pitch gain, 4 for log-gain and 50 for ten excitation vectors of 5 bits each.

A BV32 frame covers 80 samples at 16000 samples per second and is encoded as 160 bits, or 20 octets. It uses 17 bits for Line Spectrum Pairs (7+5+5), 8 for pitch lag, 5 for pitch gain, 10 for two log-gains (5+5) and 120 for twenty excitation vectors of 6 bits (two subframes of ten). Bits are packed in network byte order, most significant bit first.
sections.plainLanguage: Each slice has a fixed set of boxes for different pieces of the sound, always packed in the same order so the receiver knows where to look.

sections.title: Multiple Frames per Packet
sections.content:
A sender MAY include more than one frame in a packet but SHOULD NOT include more than fit in the RTP MTU, MUST NOT split a frame between packets, and MUST keep the frames consecutive. Because frames are a fixed 5 ms, the timestamp of the frame N frames after the oldest is the packet timestamp plus 5*N ms in time units.

The number of frames is not sent. The receiver counts the payload octets and divides by 10 for BV16 or 20 for BV32. The RFC recommends choosing the frame count to suit the application: fewer frames lower the delay in telephony, while delay-insensitive streaming or messaging can use many.
sections.plainLanguage: You can put several slices in one envelope, as long as none are torn and they go in order. Fewer slices means faster mail; more slices means fewer envelopes.

sections.title: MIME and SDP Mapping
sections.content:
Two MIME subtypes, audio/BV16 and audio/BV32, were registered in the IETF tree. They have optional parameters ptime and maxptime, and maxptime SHOULD be a multiple of the 5 ms frame duration. The intended usage is listed as COMMON.

In SDP, the MIME type goes in the m= line, the subtype goes in a=rtpmap as the encoding name, and the clock rate MUST be 8000 for BV16 and 16000 for BV32. The RFC says no special considerations are needed for the SDP Offer/Answer model.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the name tags that tell the other side which kind of voice squeezing is inside the packets and how fast the clock ticks.

sections.title: Security and Congestion Control
sections.content:
These packets inherit the security considerations of RTP and the applicable profile, so confidentiality is achieved by encryption. A denial-of-service risk exists for codecs with non-uniform decoding load, but the RFC says these encodings do not exhibit any significant non-uniformity.

General RTP congestion control applies. BV16 and BV32 have no built-in way to reduce bandwidth. Packing more frames per packet cuts IP/UDP/RTP header overhead, at the cost of more delay and less robustness against packet loss.
sections.plainLanguage: To keep a call private you lock the envelopes. And if the mail road gets crowded, stuffing more slices per envelope saves envelopes but makes you wait longer.
